## Style guides

A **style guide** is a set of rules and conventions for writing code. They cover topics like naming, code layout, syntax, docstrings, indentation. They help standardise code and improve readability.

![](linting_resources/style_guides.png){width=40% fig-align="center"}

:::{.python-content}
Popular python style guides include:

* [**PEP-8**](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/) - the **official style guide** for Python. This is supported by other Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) documents, like [PEP-257](https://peps.python.org/pep-0257/) which outlines [docstring](docstrings.qmd) conventions.

* [**Google Python Style Guide**](https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html) - used at google.
:::

:::{.r-content}
Popular R style guides include:

* [**Tidyverse style guide**](https://style.tidyverse.org/) - developed by the tidyverse team (creators of packages like `dplyr`).

* [**Google style guide**](https://google.github.io/styleguide/Rguide.html) - adapted from the tidyverse guide for used at google.
:::

You are not required to follow style guides, but they are recommended for writing clear, maintainable, and consistent code. The easiest way to enforce their requirements is using linters or code formatters.

<br>

## Linters

**Linters** are tools that analyse code for:

* **Possible errors** - looking for issues like unused variables and code complexity.
* **Style issues** - enforcing requirements from style guides.

They are often run from the command line, and return a list of suggestions for you to address. Sometimes, they might flag code that you have intentionally written, and it's okay to disagree with their suggestion to change it!

![](linting_resources/linting.png){width=60% fig-align="center"}

:::::{.python-content}

Popular linters in Python include:

* [**pylint**](https://pypi.org/project/pylint/) - checks for a **wide range of problems** include code correctness, best practices, and some style issues.

* [**flake8**](https://pypi.org/project/flake8/) - focuses mainly on enforcing **style guidelines, especially PEP-8**. It is stricter about formatting and whitespace but checks fewer aspects of code correctness.

You can use both linters together, or choose one that suits you best.

To better understand their differences, let's run them on a some poor quality code. We can see that:

* Both identify the trailing whitespace.
* Pylint identifies the missing module and function docstrings, and the function name.
* Flake8 identifies the missing whitespace around an operator.

`code.py`:

```{.python}
{{< include linting_resources/code.py >}}
```

```{.python}

```

```{python}
#| echo: false

result = subprocess.run(
    ["pylint", "linting_resources/code.py"],
    capture_output=True, text=True
)
print(result.stdout)
```

:::
:::{.column width="5%"}
:::
:::{.column width="47.5%"}
Flake8:

```{.python}
flake8 linting_resources/code.py
```

```{python}
#| echo: false

result = subprocess.run(
    ["flake8", "linting_resources/code.py"],
    capture_output=True, text=True
)
print(result.stdout)
```
:::
::::

:::::

:::{.r-content}
In R, the most popular and main option for linting is  [**lintr**](https://lintr.r-lib.org/). It enforces the tidyverse style guide, along with identifying some other wider issues like around efficiency and robustness. 

As an example, we can run lintr on some poor quality code:

```{.R}
{{< include linting_resources/code.R >}}
```

Lintr is executed from the R console:

```{r}
lintr::lint("linting_resources/code.R")
```

:::

## Code formatters

**Code formatters** are tools that automatically format your code. They are typically designed to address **code style** (e.g. following style guidelines), rather than some of the wider issues that might be flagged by linters.

![](linting_resources/code_formatters.png){width=90% fig-align="center"}

:::{.python-content}
Popular code formatters in Python include:

* [**black**](https://github.com/psf/black) - very popular code formatter.

* [**ruff**](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff) - designed to be a drop-in replacement for `black` that should have a near identical output, but runs faster.

As an example, if we ran either of these code formatters on our example by executing `black linting_resources/code.py` or `ruff format linting_resources/code.py`, they would alter the file as follows:

```{python}
#| echo: false

result = subprocess.run(
    ["black", "--diff", "--color", "linting_resources/code.py"],
    capture_output=True, text=True
)

# Convert ANSI-coloured output to html
conv = Ansi2HTMLConverter(dark_bg=False)
html_output = conv.convert(result.stdout)

# Remove datetime
html_output = re.sub(
    r'(<span class="ansi1">[-+]{3}\s[^\s]+)\s+\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}.*?</span>',
    r'\1</span>',
    html_output
)

# Remove <body> tags, background-color styles, global font and margin settings
# (as they will alter the quarto page)
html_output = re.sub(r'<body.*?>', '', html_output, flags=re.DOTALL)
html_output = html_output.replace('</body>', '')
html_output = re.sub(r'background-color: ?#[0-9a-fA-F]{6};?', '', html_output)
html_output = re.sub(r'margin: ?0;?', '', html_output)
html_output = re.sub(r'font-family:.*?;', '', html_output)

# Display
HTML(html_output)
```

:::

:::{.r-content}
Code formatters in R include:

* [**styler**](https://styler.r-lib.org/) - implements the tidyverse style guide (or can be customised to a different style).

* [**formatR**](https://yihui.org/formatr/) - designed to improve readability (e.g. addressing spaces, indentation, line breaks).

* [**air**](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/) - faster, modern code formatter (in beta as of June 2025).
:::
